lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: You two, Trophonius and Amphilochus — I have never understood how, being dead, you qualified for temples and a reputation as prophets. The useless sort of living people have actually decided you are gods.

lines.speaker: Amphilochus
lines.text: And how is that our fault, if their stupidity leads them to hold such opinions about dead men?

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: They would not hold them if, while you were alive, you had not been putting on this same sort of circus act — pretending you knew the future in advance and could tell it to anyone who asked.

lines.speaker: Trophonius
lines.text: Menippus, Amphilochus here can answer for himself. As for me: I am a hero, and I deliver oracles when someone comes down to me. You plainly have never visited Lebadeia at all. Otherwise you would not be so sceptical.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: What are you saying? Unless I go to Lebadeia, dress myself up absurdly in linen, take a barley-cake in both hands, and crawl through that low little mouth into the cave, I cannot know that you are dead like the rest of us, differing only by the stage-magic? But — in the name of prophecy — what exactly is a hero? I ask because I have no idea.

lines.speaker: Trophonius
lines.text: A kind of compound: part man, part god.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Something that is neither man, as you say, nor god, and yet both at once. Right. So where has this god-half of yours gone now?

lines.speaker: Trophonius
lines.text: It gives oracles, Menippus. In Boeotia.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: I do not know what you think you are saying, Trophonius. What I can see perfectly well is that the whole of you is dead.
